column1: What is the central invariant governing professional document architecture?
column2: The separation of semantic structure from visual formatting—content and presentation must remain decoupled so documents stay machine-readable, accessible, and portable across output formats.

column1: Why is a heading in a properly structured document not 'just bold 18-point text'?
column2: It exists as a semantically tagged object carrying hierarchical level information, outline position, cross-reference anchoring capability, and table-of-contents generation metadata.

column1: What happens when authors apply direct character formatting instead of semantic styles?
column2: The document devolves into a brittle, non-portable artifact that resists automation, breaks under version control stress, and fails accessibility compliance audits.

column1: What is the core architectural reality that distinguishes modern documents from typewriter-era text?
column2: Modern documents are object models—a structured data graph (tree of objects with typed relationships, embedded metadata, programmatic behaviors)—rather than a linear, irreversible character stream.

column1: What is the key formatting invariant stated for professional documentation workflows?
column2: Direct formatting is technical debt, while style-based formatting is programmatic infrastructure.

column1: Describe the style resolution pipeline that determines a document element's final visual properties.
column2: A deterministic cascade: document defaults → theme definitions → inherited style specifications → local (direct) overrides.

column1: Why do long-form business documents default to serif typefaces for body text, while headings use sans-serif?
column2: Serif faces create implicit baseline guides that reduce saccadic eye movement cost during extended reading; sans-serif faces offer geometric clarity that survives low-resolution display and signals hierarchy unambiguously.

column1: What is the recommended line spacing (leading) range for body text relative to point size?
column2: Approximately 120% to 145% of the point size.

column1: What distributed-systems trade-off underlies all collaborative document editing models?
column2: Consistency versus availability—prioritizing immediate responsiveness (allowing divergent edits needing later reconciliation) versus strict consistency (serializing changes through central authority at the cost of latency).

column1: What is the core invariant underlying all document collaboration models?
column2: Preservation of authorial intent across temporal and spatial boundaries—distinguishing original content, suggestions, and acceptances/rejections via explicit change-tracking, comment threading, and version ancestry structures.

column1: Why does document version control differ fundamentally from source code version control?
column2: Documents have semantic units (sentences, paragraphs, sections) that resist clean line-based diffing; a single change can ripple through dependent clauses, headings, or the table of contents, requiring structure-aware (DOM-level) versioning rather than byte-level differencing.

column1: What are the three architectural pillars of Word's automation capability, and what is the governing invariant for all automation architectures?
column2: Pillars: (1) the Document Object Model exposing programmable elements, (2) field codes providing declarative templating, (3) Open XML format enabling external XML-based generation/parsing. Governing invariant: idempotency and state transparency.
